description: Learning all about computational physics and computer science.
summary:
Lumen: Space Fire Explorer is an AI-powered dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into a parsable summary of key results, with a focus on fire safety. It draws on 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s PSI database, 586 fire tests and 187 NASA reports and papers, which it ranks, summarises and interprets with a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) AI. Users can learn how fire behaves at different gravitational field strengths, explore PSI experiments ranked for a habitat of their choosing, get a fire risk briefing for any cabin atmosphere, replay real Saffire fires in an Orion-sized cabin to see when carbon monoxide reaches NASA’s limits, and download the test data as CSV for modelling. Lumen, the AI assistant, answers in simple or scientific mode, cites every claim with a relevance percentage, and declines when NASA’s data doesn’t cover the query.

This matters for a future Moon base. NASA plans a 34% oxygen atmosphere at 8.2 psia, where 15 of 22 tested spacecraft materials keep burning in NASA’s Earth-gravity tests, yet no test has been run in that atmosphere at lunar gravity. Lumen shows where those gaps are and points to the experiment that would close them, such as NASA’s upcoming Flammability of Materials on the Moon test.
details:
NOTE: The website is not optimised for mobile viewing, it will perform best on a laptop. Additionally, without regular traffic google cloud may take a moment to load the site.

Who we are

We are a team of four multi-university STEM students, from the University of Cambridge, Imperial College London, Durham University and Charles University, taking part in our first Space Apps Challenge. With collective experience in physics, mathematics and computer science, and with two of our team members having already built rudimentary RAG chatbots during internships, the microgravity combustion challenge was the best choice for our expertise. The physicists took the combustion science, mathematicians designed our ranking system and computer scientists built the dashboard and centre piece - Lumen, the AI research assistant. 

What it does and how it works

Lumen: Space Fire Explorer is an AI powered dashboard about how fire behaves in microgravity and how to keep crews safe from it. It is built for engineers, scientists and curious members of the public. The knowledge base comes from NASA sources: the 24 combustion investigations in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, 586 fire test records from ISS and Saffire experiments, 187 reports, papers and documents. The site has six primary parts, outlined below:

Fire In Microgravity: 

A guide on how gravity, oxygen, pressure and airflow change fire compared to typical earth combustion and how crews detect and put out fires in space. This is supplemented by graphs using NASA data, with accessible references to all source material, on top of a simulation of a candle flame in varying gravitational field strengths. 

NASA Experiments:

A list of all 24 PSI investigations ranked by relevance for your chosen habitat. There are numerous habitats to explore from the ISS to a mars atmosphere, with the option to create your own custom environment. Any significant gap in data is outlined. 

Habitat Fire Risk: 

Choose your own habitat, with the custom option available, and explore the potential fire risks. The tool ranks 41 curated findings by how close their test conditions match and how strong the evidence is, showing the materials which would burn and where no tests exist. Experiments are then proposed that would close the biggest gap in the data, if there is one.

Cabin Fire Replay: 

A simulation of a real Saffire fire with the user's chosen material, cabin size, and smoke detector limit. The carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide levels are monitored as a function of time with a graph outlining NASAs safe threshold and at what time it is breached. 

Lumen, the AI research assistant:

Lumen searches NASA sources by meaning and by keyword, reranks the results and uses lookup tools for exact figures. Each answer cites its sources and gives each a relevance percentage to the question asked. Users pick simple or scientists mode, with the latter using terminology a researcher may be more familiar with. Lumen also supports transcription and answers read aloud to allow the assistant to be accessible to everyone.

Data downloads:

Every test record can be filtered and downloaded as a CSV. 

Benefits and impact

Decades of NASA research is scattered across the internet, Lumen brings them together to answer any query you may have without having to scour thousands of documents. We make it our priority to show where there are data gaps instead of hiding them, with suggestions of how to improve the missing gaps. One key piece of information uncovered, has been the absence of experiments in a moon base environment. This will be of vital importance for the upcoming Artemis missions. Our project suggests potential experiments which could be done to plug the gaps in the current research. Lumen should offer an easy way for scientists to find the experiments most relevant to their work and offer clear insight into the safest materials and risks for a given atmosphere. It should also help assist anyone curious into learning more about combustion, with simulations and guides on this topic. 

Technicals

Language: Python and JavaScript.

Backend: Flask.

Search and retrieval: ChromaDB, BM25 keyword search, and local embedding and reranking models (BAAI bge-small and MiniLM) that run on an ordinary CPU.

AI: Claude. Haiku 5.5 for Lumen.

PDF extraction: pdfplumber and pypdf.

Frontend: Plotly for charts, KaTeX for formulas, and a WebGL2 flame simulation that runs on the viewer’s GPU.

Voice: the browser’s speech recognition for spoken questions, and ElevenLabs for reading answers aloud.

Testing: pytest, plus our own set of test questions for the AI.

Hardware: nothing special. Everything runs on a standard laptop.

Creativity

Flame simulation: 

A gravity slider allows the user to explore how a candle flame changes in different gravitational field strengths. It is a reacting flow simulation, not an animation. 

AI as an experiment designer:

Besides just answering questions, Lumen proposes new experiments to try and plug the gaps in the present research. 

Charts from real data:

Charts can be displayed in the Lumen chatbot, which help supplement the user's query. The AI never generates chart numbers - every datum is a recorded NASA result

Lumen’s look:

Lumen was intended to be somewhat reminiscent of HAL 9000 from 2001: A Space Odyssey (though not evil!), hence the circular image of a flame in microgravity. In the chat, the flame pulses as Lumen speaks. 

A familiar theme:

The site is typeset like a LaTeX paper, with the general theme of the website being similar to a research paper.

Factors we considered

Accuracy:

The assistant was tested on 39 questions which we knew the answers to. In both modes, 33 out of the 34 relevant questions cited a correct source and the 5 off topic questions where declined. 

Honesty about limitations:

Estimates are marked and the flame simulation is labelled as illustrative. Though Lumen passed 33/34 questions, the user should be wary of responses and for absolute certainty read the source material. 

Transparency:

A methods page shows where AI is and is not used, how the findings are ranked and all the resources we used. 

Cost:

Only the chatbot actively calls the anthropic API, and the graphs are pre-generated for Lumen to call. The assistant also runs using the cheapest model of Claude, Haiku, costing less than 1p per question. 

Accessibility:
With intent to make the website as usable to anyone who wishes, we created the two answer modes, voice input and narration for Lumen.

Goodbye

We thoroughly hope you enjoy this project, we have had a great time making it - not only learning some complicated physics, but also learning about website creation, and using artificial intelligence in a scientific setting. Enjoy!
